extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of speculative fiction (authors, editors, critics) interested in subgenre classification
extracted.subtask_description: Define and characterize the proposed subgenre 'curio fiction' — realistic-world speculative stories built around a single unusual element — to help readers, writers, and critics identify and label such works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curio fiction — simple definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A story set in a world identical or similar to our own (contemporary, historical, or near-future) with a twist — an added fantasy, science fiction, or horror element that is examined for its effect on the story's human characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the article's central definition: curio fiction fits under speculative fiction but emphasizes an otherwise-real world made strange by a single or limited speculative element. Example works: The Midnight Library, Pushing Daisies, The Invisible Life of Addie LaRue. Note: categories overlap and not all works will fit neatly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-world setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Takes place in a real-world setting (need not be a specific named place; can be historical or near-future) and more closely mirrors the logic and human experience of a realistic world than surrealist or absurdist fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Frances Hardinge's The Lie Tree (Victorian-era island) and contemporary/near-future settings. Anti-pattern: fully secondary/worldbuilding-heavy fantasies that create an entire alternate world (e.g., most high fantasy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Story-defining speculative element (the curio) — 'one notch off' from reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative centers on a single, story-defining speculative element — a curio — that is 'one notch off' from reality (a strange place, person with an unusual power, or mysterious item) and is examined for its effect on human characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The curio can be magical or technological; it may be integrated into society or perceived as unusual. Examples: time-loop stories (Groundhog Day), body-swap (Freaky Friday), a device counting down to your soulmate (TiMER), out-of-body experience (If I Stay). The curio is the vehicle for the 'what if' thought experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curio is not usually defined as part of a global system; limited/worldbuilding-localized
rubrics_metrics.description: The speculative element typically isn't explained as part of a global, rule-driven system; authors often hand-wave scientific explanations or avoid detailing larger-system mechanics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worldbuilding is smaller in scale and localized to one character or area rather than building an expansive setting (contrast with Marvel or Harry Potter). Example: Rebecca Serle's In Five Years — protagonist travels to her future but the mechanism is unexplained. Anti-pattern: immersive fantasy with structured magic rules and extensive systemic worldbuilding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humans are the primary focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Curio fiction centers on human capabilities and experiences rather than on fantastical species or nonhuman societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes curio fiction from subgenres featuring dragons, elves, aliens, or robot cultures. Example: The Cartographers focuses on human-centered magical mapmaking. Anti-pattern: urban fantasy dominated by vampires, werewolves, or fae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on effects on relationships and social systems over mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: The story prioritizes how the curio affects relationships, desires, fears, moral choices, and social structures rather than explaining how or why the curio exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often functions as a philosophical thought experiment (time, memory, death, free will); may be more conversation-based than action-based (examples: The Man from Earth, The Booth at the End). The curio intensifies preexisting human desires and conflicts. Anti-pattern: narratives that focus on discovering or exploiting the curio's mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curio functions as a novum/novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopts Suvin's 'novum' idea: the curio is the novel deviation from reality that allows the narrative to interrogate real-world questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the curio as the 'new thing' whose presence reframes the familiar world. Use the curio to underscore a concept and narrow the story's scope (example: The Time Traveler's Wife uses chrono-displacement to examine time and relationships).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre and tone flexibility; cross-genre applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Curio fiction can cross or combine genres (romance, thriller, horror, dark comedy, near-future tech) and can be light or dark in tone; the defining quality is the single odd element and its human-centered exploration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples across forms: romantic fantasy (TiMER), thriller (The Dead Zone), dark comedy (The Brass Teapot), near-future tech (They Both Die at the End), films/TV (Black Mirror, Eternal Sunshine). The label should be inclusive of fantasy, soft sci‑fi, and horror varieties when they meet curio criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not magical realism (distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Curio fiction should not be conflated with magical realism, which historically and critically is tied to postcolonial contexts and specific literary traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magical realism keystones (One Hundred Years of Solitude, Midnight's Children, Beloved) address postcolonial themes; curio fiction's magic is usually treated as surprising or localized rather than a comment grounded in those traditions. Anti-pattern: labeling works as magical realism without regard for cultural/critical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not fabulism or surrealism (distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Curio fiction differs from fabulism/surrealism, which often produce prose and worlds as surreal or absurd as the events themselves; curio fiction remains grounded in realistic logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabulism examples (Alice, Invisible Cities) are more mythic/surreal; curio stories keep characters, prose, and reader logic anchored to the familiar while introducing a singular oddity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'low', 'soft', or 'light' labels as primary descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like low fantasy, soft sci‑fi, or light speculative fiction carry ambiguous meanings or value judgments and don't clearly capture the specific quality of a realistic world with one odd element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article argues these labels are either too broad, imply hierarchies (low/high), or suggest tone (light) that may not apply. Use a term (e.g., 'curio fiction') that signals the story's concern with effect over cause and the presence of a single curio, rather than implying inferiority or insufficient genre-ness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming/label criterion — term should be immediately evocative
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing a subgenre label, prefer terms whose meaning is immediately understood or felt, evoking the concept (e.g., 'curio' suggests cabinets of strange delights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author chose 'curio fiction' because Merriam-Webster's curio = 'something considered novel, rare, or bizarre' and the word evokes curiosity shops and strange delights. A good label helps audiences find works and sets reader expectations about emphasis (effect > cause).
